KOL Campaigns Need More Than Impression Screenshots

By lowob · 16 August 2026 · Updated 9 November 2026 · 6-minute read · Growth / Crypto

The standard Web3 creator report looks impressive until someone asks what changed. Reach is visible. Commercial impact is usually harder to prove.

A screenshot of impressions demonstrates distribution, not product understanding or adoption. The more useful question is whether the creator brought a relevant audience to a specific action and whether that behavior persisted after the campaign ended.

This is as much a buying problem as a tracking problem. A team can commission a campaign before defining whom it needs to reach, what the audience should do, or how the result will be measured.

84.4%

of surveyed Web3 companies used paid KOL campaigns in 2025

25%

did not track marketing or user-acquisition costs in 2025

7.6%

selected follower count as a reason to choose a KOL

Source: Green Dots, 2025 to 2026 Web3 Marketing Study, based on a survey of more than 150 crypto companies. These are survey responses, not performance benchmarks or lowob campaign results.

KOL is the default. That doesn't make it effective.

Green Dots found paid creator promotion was the most commonly used marketing format among its respondents. But one in four companies in that same survey said they didn't track marketing or acquisition costs. That combination should concern anyone approving a creator budget: a widely adopted channel can still be poorly measured.

The buying pattern also matters. In the survey, 53.1% said their marketing spend concentrated around major events, while 26.6% maintained recurring monthly budgets. That often leaves a creator with one launch window to establish context, explain a product and convert a skeptical audience.

This doesn't mean KOL relationships are inherently ineffective. It means a launch-day spike is a weak basis for declaring success. Recurring creator partnerships may make sense when the story is worth revisiting and there is evidence that audiences become more qualified over time.

Define the job before choosing the voice

Start with the intended outcome. A staking product might need users to connect a wallet and delegate. An infrastructure team might need credible developers to try an integration. A tokenized-asset provider might need informed conversations with a small set of decision-makers. Those are not interchangeable audiences or actions.

Creator selection should follow the job. In Green Dots' survey, 66% of respondents selected reputation as a criterion and 56.6% selected research or content quality; only 7.6% selected follower count. The sample suggests teams increasingly say they value credibility, but a media kit alone cannot demonstrate whether an audience will act.

Look at who engages, the questions they ask, whether the creator actually understands the product and whether their previous sponsored relationships create conflicts. A focused technical creator may create less total attention but more valuable actions than a generalist account with a larger audience.

Connect the click to the action

The most consequential measurement gap in DeFi is between a campaign click and what a wallet subsequently does. As Formo's KOL measurement framework explains, ordinary web analytics can show a visit and referral source, but those records do not automatically establish which wallet later completed a swap, deposit or other onchain action.

Set the measurement plan before activation. Give each creator and placement an identifiable link; persist campaign context across the visit and wallet connection where technically and legally appropriate; then measure first meaningful action and subsequent behavior.

Consider someone who clicks a creator's link on X, reads about a lending protocol, and leaves. Two days later, they return, connect a wallet and make a deposit. A normal website report may record the first visit without knowing which wallet made that deposit. Formo describes how to bridge that gap: give each creator a distinct campaign link, save its source information in the visitor's browser, then connect that information to the wallet address when the person connects. The project can then check whether that wallet actually deposited assets, swapped tokens or returned later. This only works when the visit and wallet connection can reliably be linked; different devices, lost browser data or privacy choices can leave gaps.

Follow the signal

Four distinct checks, from distribution to whether the spend was worth repeating.

Distribution

Qualified views, referral visits, audience relevance

Did the message reach people who might actually use the product?

Activation

Attributed wallet connections, first deposits, swaps or other product actions

Did a referral become meaningful product use?

Durability

Seven- and 30-day cohorts, repeat actions, retained value

Did activity continue once the incentive or campaign ended?

Economics

Full channel spend divided by verified activated users, compared with alternatives

Is there evidence to invest in this creator again?

Measurement framework informed by Formo's attribution guidance and lowob's recommended commercial decision criteria. This table is a methodology, not reported campaign results.

Better tracking changes which creators deserve more money. Formo gives an illustrative comparison, not a client case study: one creator brings 400 wallet connections, but only 12% complete a first transaction; another brings 150 connections, with 31% completing a first transaction. That's roughly the same number of first transactions despite very different traffic numbers. Formo's example also shows 30-day retention of 18% versus 34%. If the campaign costs and audience goals are similar, the second creator deserves a closer look for future spending. A team should still examine actual deposits or trading activity, repeat use and total campaign costs before renewing anyone.

A wallet is not necessarily a person, and a connection is not necessarily a customer. One person may use multiple wallets; incentives can attract short-lived activity. Attribution may remain partial. State which outcomes are directly observed, which are inferred and which remain unknown.

A useful KOL report should make it possible to cut, renew or redesign the next campaign. If it only proves content was delivered, it is a fulfilment report.

Price the full cost of acquisition

A creator fee is only part of the acquisition cost. Include briefing, strategy, editing, management time, event support, incentives, data tooling and moderation. Use the same cost basis when comparing KOLs against partnerships, founder-led education, organic research, affiliate distribution or paid media.

Green Dots found that nearly 60% of its respondents targeted customer acquisition cost below $30. That is a statement about expectations, not evidence that $30 is a realistic acquisition cost for a particular DeFi product. The meaningful comparison is the cost of retained, valuable users, with conversion definitions and attribution limits explained.

Formo recommends cost per activated wallet as a more useful operational metric than cost per click. We agree, with a qualification: it should be paired with retention, wallet quality and downstream value. Otherwise, a campaign optimized for activation can simply purchase the cheapest one-time action.

lowob takeaways

  • Buy a defined behavior, not a creator's follower count. Product education, a first deposit and an institutional conversation require different creators, landing experiences and success measures.
  • Instrument the conversion before paying for distribution. A creator-specific link that loses attribution before wallet connection gives you a traffic report, not a credible acquisition report.
  • Make the second payment conditional on evidence. A briefing and small activation can test the audience before a multi-post retainer. Look for useful actions and retention, not a one-day impression spike.
  • Compare fixed-fee KOL spend with accountable alternatives. Where a conversion can be verified, referral, affiliate or partner arrangements may align payment more closely with value. Guard against gaming and don't mistake attributed wallets for unique customers.

Sources and methodology

Green Dots: Web3 User Acquisition: Why CAC Expectations Are Broken (4 May 2026). Survey of 150+ crypto companies covering channel use, creator selection, budgets and CAC expectations. Survey findings are descriptive and not industry-wide causal estimates.

Formo: Why KOL Campaigns Fail in DeFi: Key Metrics and Measurement Framework (15 June 2026; updated 1 September 2026). Referenced for offchain-to-onchain attribution, wallet activation, cohort retention and cost-per-activated-wallet methodology.
